content: The term maternal and child health refers to the health and well-being of mothers and their children, encompassing a range of medical, social, and public health interventions aimed at improving outcomes for both. Nucleic acid testing (NAT) is a highly sensitive diagnostic method used to detect the presence of specific genetic material, such as viral RNA or DNA, in a sample. It is commonly employed in the diagnosis of infectious diseases, including HIV. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) are independent entities that operate outside of government control, often focusing on humanitarian, developmental, or advocacy work in various sectors, including health. Negative predictive value (NPV) is a statistical measure that indicates the likelihood that a person with a negative test result truly does not have the disease being tested for. National regulatory authorities (NRAs) are government agencies responsible for ensuring the safety, efficacy, and quality of medical products, including diagnostics and treatments, within their jurisdiction. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) refers to the administration of antiretroviral medications after potential exposure to HIV to prevent infection. The U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) is a global initiative led by the United States to combat the HIV/AIDS epidemic through funding, treatment, and prevention programs. The PICO framework (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) is a structured approach used in evidence-based medicine to formulate clinical questions and guide systematic reviews. Provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) involves healthcare providers offering HIV testing and counseling as part of routine medical care, particularly in settings with a high prevalence of HIV. Prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV includes interventions such as antiretroviral therapy to prevent the transmission of HIV from an infected mother to her child during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding. Point-of-care (POC) testing refers to diagnostic tests performed at or near the site of patient care, providing rapid results to facilitate immediate clinical decision-making. Positive predictive value (PPV) is a statistical measure that indicates the likelihood that a person with a positive test result truly has the disease being tested for. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) involves the use of antiretroviral medications by individuals at high risk of HIV infection to prevent acquiring the virus. Proficiency testing (PT) is a quality assurance measure in which laboratories are evaluated on their ability to accurately perform diagnostic tests by analyzing standardized samples. Quality assurance (QA) encompasses systematic processes and procedures to ensure that healthcare services, including diagnostic testing, meet established standards of quality and reliability. Quality control (QC) refers to the operational techniques and activities used to monitor and maintain the quality of diagnostic tests and laboratory processes. Quality improvement (QI) involves continuous efforts to enhance healthcare services, including diagnostic testing, by identifying and addressing areas for improvement. Quality management systems (QMS) are comprehensive frameworks that integrate quality assurance, quality control, and quality improvement processes to ensure the consistent delivery of high-quality healthcare services. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are experimental studies in which participants are randomly assigned to intervention or control groups to evaluate the efficacy of a treatment or intervention. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are simple, quick, and portable diagnostic tools used to detect specific diseases, such as HIV or syphilis, often in resource-limited settings. Recent infection testing algorithms (RITAs) are diagnostic strategies used to identify individuals with recent HIV infections, which can inform public health interventions and surveillance. Reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health (RMNCH) encompasses a broad range of healthcare services aimed at improving the health and well-being of women, infants, and children. HIV Rapid Test Continuous Quality Improvement (RTCQI) programs focus on enhancing the quality and reliability of rapid HIV testing through ongoing monitoring and improvement initiatives. Strategic Evaluation Advisory & Development Consulting (SEAD) is a consulting entity that provides expertise in evaluating and developing strategies for healthcare programs and interventions. Steering groups (SGs) are committees or panels that provide guidance and oversight for the development and implementation of healthcare policies, programs, or guidelines. Short messaging service (SMS) refers to text messaging technology that can be used in healthcare for patient communication, appointment reminders, and health education. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) are detailed, written instructions that outline standardized processes for performing specific tasks or procedures in healthcare settings. The Stepwise Process for Improving the Quality of HIV Rapid Testing (SPI-RT) is a structured approach to enhance the quality and reliability of rapid HIV testing services. Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) encompasses healthcare services and interventions related to sexual health, family planning, and reproductive health. Syphilis self-testing (SST) allows individuals to test themselves for syphilis using a self-administered diagnostic kit, increasing access to testing services. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections transmitted primarily through sexual contact, including HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, and chlamydia. Treatment-adjusted prevalence (TAP) refers to the prevalence of a disease, such as HIV, adjusted for the proportion of individuals receiving treatment. Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, primarily affecting the lungs but potentially impacting other parts of the body. Treponemal tests (TP) are diagnostic tests used to detect antibodies specific to Treponema pallidum, the bacterium that causes syphilis. The concept of Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U) emphasizes that individuals with HIV who achieve and maintain an undetectable viral load through antiretroviral therapy cannot transmit the virus to their sexual partners. Universal health coverage (UHC) aims to ensure that all individuals have access to essential healthcare services without financial hardship. The United Nations (UN) is an international organization that promotes global peace, security, and development, including efforts to combat HIV/AIDS. The Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) coordinates global efforts to end the HIV/AIDS epidemic through advocacy, funding, and technical support. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) focuses on global development initiatives, including addressing health challenges such as HIV/AIDS. The United States Agency for International Development (USAID) is a U.S. government agency that provides international development assistance, including funding for global health programs. Voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) involves individuals voluntarily seeking HIV testing and counseling services, often in a supportive and confidential environment. Viral load (VL) refers to the amount of HIV RNA present in a person’s blood, which is a key indicator of disease progression and treatment efficacy. Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) is a preventive intervention that reduces the risk of heterosexual HIV transmission in men. The World Health Organization (WHO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for international public health. The executive summary of the WHO guidelines on differentiated HIV testing services (HTS) highlights the integration of existing and new evidence-based approaches to improve HIV testing across diverse settings and populations. The guidelines emphasize the importance of achieving the global 95-95-95 targets, which aim to diagnose 95% of all people with HIV, provide antiretroviral therapy to 95% of those diagnosed, and achieve viral suppression in 95% of those treated. The WHO recommends expanding access to self-testing, network-based testing services, and other innovative approaches to enhance HIV testing coverage and linkage to care. The guidelines also address the need for quality assurance, strategic planning, and tailored interventions to reach priority populations, including men, adolescents, pregnant women, and key populations at high risk of HIV. The WHO underscores the importance of integrating HIV testing with other health services, such as syphilis testing, and leveraging virtual platforms to improve access and uptake. The guidelines aim to support countries in closing the HIV testing gap, reducing new infections, and achieving global targets to end the HIV epidemic as a public health threat by 2030.
